summary: Hebrew masculine nouns usually take -im (ים), feminine nouns -ot (וֹת); the vowels of the stem often change.

askYourself: Do the stem vowels shorten (גֶּזֶר → גְּזָרִים)?

traps: The ending does not always follow the gender: דְּלַעַת (pumpkin) is feminine, yet its plural is דְּלוּעִים (-im).
The stem vowels change in the plural: גֶּזֶר → גְּזָרִים, בָּצָל → בְּצָלִים.

notes.text: As in Greek, the plural ending depends on the noun (-οι, -ες, -α ~ -ִים, -וֹת) and must be learnt with it; Hebrew adds vowel changes inside the stem (סֵפֶר → סְפָרִים).
As in Russian, the ending depends on the noun and the stem can change; Hebrew has just two main endings, -ִים and -וֹת, and no case forms of the plural.
Spanish adds -s / -es to every noun; Hebrew chooses between -ִים and -וֹת, often changes the stem vowels (סֵפֶר → סְפָרִים) and keeps a dual in a few words (יוֹמַיִם).
English adds -s and has a few irregulars (man → men); in Hebrew stem changes are common (סֵפֶר → סְפָרִים, בַּיִת → בָּתִּים), so learn the plural with the word.
The French plural is mostly silent (-s); the Hebrew plural is always heard: -ִים / -וֹת, often with a vowel change in the stem.
As in German, the plural is learnt with each noun and can change the stem (Buch → Bücher ~ סֵפֶר → סְפָרִים); Hebrew has only two endings, but many stem changes.
Hindi plurals depend on gender and ending (लड़का → लड़के, लड़की → लड़कियाँ), as Hebrew ones do (-ִים / -וֹת); Hebrew also changes vowels inside the stem.
The Persian endings -ها / -ان do not depend on gender, and the noun stays singular after a number; the Hebrew ending depends on the noun, and the plural is used after every number from 2.
Marathi plurals depend on gender and ending (मुलगा → मुलगे); Hebrew too — -ִים mostly for masculine, -וֹת mostly for feminine — with stem changes.

The sound plurals -ūna / -āt match -ִים / -וֹת, but Hebrew has no broken plurals: the inside of the word changes only its vowels (סֵפֶר → סְפָרִים, not like كِتَاب → كُتُب), and the dual lives only in a few words.
Turkish has one plural suffix (-ler / -lar, by vowel harmony) and drops it after numbers (üç kitap); Hebrew has two endings, stem changes, and a plural after every number (שְׁלוֹשָׁה סְפָרִים).
Japanese nouns usually have no plural form; in Hebrew the plural is obligatory — סֵפֶר “a book”, סְפָרִים “books” — and everything that agrees becomes plural too.
Korean marks the plural only optionally (-들); in Hebrew it is obligatory whenever there is more than one.
Finnish marks the plural with -t or with -i- before a case ending; Hebrew uses -ִים / -וֹת and often changes the stem vowels.
Hungarian adds -k (könyvek) but keeps the singular after numbers; Hebrew uses -ִים / -וֹת and always the plural after numbers.
Swahili makes the plural by changing the class prefix (kitabu → vitabu, mtu → watu); Hebrew changes the ending (סֵפֶר → סְפָרִים) and often the stem vowels.
Luganda changes the class prefix for the plural (omuntu → abantu, ekitabo → ebitabo); Hebrew changes the ending: -ִים / -וֹת.
Chinese nouns do not change for number (们 only for people); in Hebrew every countable noun has a plural, and it must be used: שְׁנֵי סְפָרִים.
Vietnamese nouns do not change for number (những / các show it when needed); Hebrew nouns always take -ִים / -וֹת for more than one.
Inuktitut has singular, dual and plural endings for every noun (iglu, igluk, iglut); Hebrew has the plural for all nouns and the dual only for a few (יוֹמַיִם, עֵינַיִם).
